sources.title: Mahmoud Mokhtar (Q1459134), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-13): English label 'Mahmoud Mokhtar', description 'Egyptian sculptor (1891-1934)', human, born 10 May 1891, died 28 March 1934, citizen of Egypt, occupation sculptor, Arabic label محمود مختار, no Korean label. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Alex Dika Seggerman, 'Mahmoud Mokhtar', Mathaf Encyclopedia of Modern Arab Art, Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art, Doha (artist biography, read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls him a pioneer of modern Egyptian sculpture who joined Prince Youssef Kamal's new School of Fine Arts in its first class in 1908, graduated first in 1912 and went to Paris on a scholarship to study in Jules-Felix Coutan's studio; lived modestly in Paris and took low-paid jobs while sculpting, and at the end of the First World War briefly served as interim artistic director of the Musee Grevin wax museum; made a small model of Nahdat Misr (a peasant woman and a sphinx) for the 1920 Salon des Artistes Francais after the 1919 Revolution, and after about eight years of fundraising and unrest it was unveiled in Cairo on 20 May 1928; also lists the 1929 Khamasin, the 1930 Bernheim-Jeune show in Paris, his newspaper articles to build appreciation of art, and the Mahmoud Mokhtar Museum opened in 1952. Museum encyclopedia entry, admiring in tone.

Emad Abu Ghazi, 'The Guiding Hand: The Role of the State in Egyptian Fine Arts', translated by Shereen Moussad, RAWI issue 8, 2016 (read in full): essay on state patronage of Egyptian art that traces how the Nahdet Masr statue was commissioned after popular demand under a committee headed by the former prime minister Hussein Rushdy Pasha, carved in granite with stone moved from Aswan at the railways' expense, repeatedly halted by the palace and government, finished in winter 1927 and unveiled only in May 1928 after King Fouad's delay; that after Saad Zaghloul's death in 1927 he was commissioned for two statues, whose work was repeatedly suspended and over which later governments requested changes and sued him for breach of contract, a suit unresolved at his death in 1934; and that he sat on the 1924 Committee of Fine Arts. The essay is about the state's role in the arts, not a personal biography.

Nigel Ryan, 'Short-changed by history', Al-Ahram Weekly, issue 573, 14-20 February 2002 (review of a Cairo retrospective; archived copy read in full). Critical-leaning: says the symbolic burden of being 'the first Egyptian sculptor in two thousand years' has made his public works invisible, that the 1949 Abu Ghazi and Boctor study (source of his reported words) appeared fifteen years after his death so direct quotations deserve suspicion, that his peasant-woman limestones are schematised and Art Deco in manner, that he remained a product of conventional French training, and that his Head of a Black Girl (1910) and a portrait bust are among his strongest works; it also quotes a letter he sent a public-works official who wanted letters of good conduct before registering him as a salaried public servant while he worked on Egypt Awakening, in which he answers with a deliberately mocking list of his faults.

Paulina Przystupa, 'Unveiling the Ancient in the Modern: A historical examination of gender, nationalism, and Pharaonism in selected works by Mahmoud Mohktar, in the 1920s, and Muhammad Nagi, in 1922 and 1937' (University of Washington ResearchWorks, student research paper, 26 pages; text extracted and the sentences about Mokhtar read, not every page). Interpretive art-history paper: gives his entry to the School of Fine Arts, says the 1920 Nahdet Misr was made in Paris after the 1919 women's marches, that the editor Muhammad Husayn Haykal supported it, that some critics said its woman was not useful and Mokhtar disagreed, and that he repeatedly sculpted peasant women and a nude Isis. Student paper; used only for context, not for any row.

Mona Abdou, 'Nahdet Misr: A Sculpture That Embodies Egypt At A Glance', Egyptian Streets, 20 November 2021 (read in full): short popular piece describing the 1928 monument, its peasant woman lifting her veil and the sphinx, and saying he made it after the First World War and the 1919 Revolution. Popular summary; used for the description of the monument only.

persistence.rationale: [src_mokhtar_mathaf, src_mokhtar_rawi | 1910s-1934 | museum encyclopedia, essay on state patronage] The Mathaf entry says he lived modestly in Paris in the 1910s on low-paid jobs while continuing to sculpt, and that the 1920 model of Nahdat Misr became a monument only after about eight years of fundraising and political instability; Abu Ghazi adds that work on the granite statue was halted several times by the palace and government, that he finished it in winter 1927, and that the two Zaghloul statues he was commissioned for were repeatedly suspended and still in a lawsuit when he died. Several documented episodes of finishing work through interruptions, but most of the delays were caused by others and the two authors overlap on the same project. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.54 because the interruptions were the state's doing and his own conduct through them is inferred.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_mokhtar_mathaf, src_mokhtar_rawi, src_mokhtar_streets | 1919-1934 | museum encyclopedia, essay on state patronage, popular press] The Mathaf entry says he made the 1920 model in response to the 1919 Revolution, took part in independence demonstrations and wrote newspaper articles to build appreciation of art among intellectuals; Abu Ghazi places him on the 1924 Committee of Fine Arts that advised the state on the arts; the popular piece says he meant the monument to express the struggle for independence. The aim of work serving public life rather than private taste is documented in several places, but the descriptions of his intentions are retrospective and the sources overlap, and the review in Al-Ahram Weekly warns that the national symbolism later swamped the sculpture. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.5 because the purpose behind the monument is stated by later writers.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_mokhtar_mathaf | 1910s-1918 | museum encyclopedia] The Mathaf entry says that during the 1910s he lived modestly in Paris on low-paid jobs and that at the end of the First World War he briefly served as interim artistic director of the Musee Grevin, making wax figures of statesmen and performers. One source, with no detail of how he found or used these openings, so only an inference. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 56 / 0.4 because the whole claim rests on a single sentence of one entry.

portrait.reason: No defensible lifetime portrait could be verified after one bounded retry. The only candidate, Commons 'Mahmoud Mokhtar.jpg' (593 x 803, sepia photographic print, side view in a beret, uploaded January 2026, creator given as the magazine Rose al-Yusuf and date 1930, source a news-site article whose page returned 403), has no inscription or caption to confirm the sitter, no verified publication (the image is a photographic print, not a magazine page), no named photographer and no holder record, so the Rose al-Yusuf and 1930 claims cannot be checked; the PD-Egypt template rests on that unverified attribution. Alternative routes: the Commons category holds no other portrait; the 1912 studio photograph and other photographs of Mokhtar seen at Yale MAVCOR and Smarthistory are courtesy of the Mahmoud Mukhtar Archive (Dr Emad Abou-Ghazi), a private holder with no open licence found; Gallica (Cloudflare wall), Smarthistory (403) and the Internet Archive (no pre-1936 periodicals with Mokhtar found) gave nothing usable. Next step if pursued: ask the Mahmoud Mukhtar Archive or the Mahmoud Mokhtar Museum for a licensed photograph, or find a 1920s-30s printed portrait with a caption in a digitised Egyptian or French periodical.

ATTRIBUTION: limited_but_usable; the career facts (training, Paris, the monument, the Zaghloul statues, the lawsuit) are dated and well sourced, but almost no first-hand behavioural evidence survives in open sources and what exists comes through retrospective writers (the 1949 Abu Ghazi and Boctor study is quoted second-hand and flagged as suspect by Ryan). READ: Mathaf entry (full), Rawi essay (full), Al-Ahram Weekly review (full, archived), Egyptian Streets (full), the University of Washington student paper (sentences naming him), the Routledge Encyclopedia of Modernism (visible abstract only, not cited), the Yale MAVCOR catalogue entry (metadata only). NOT OPENED: Smarthistory (403), Dafbeirut (403), the Khamseen article (403), the 1993 UNESCO Courier piece by Magdi Youssef, the Mahmoud Mokhtar Museum, Karnouk's book. NOT CARDED: the precocious-child mud-figurine and 'walked into the school' stories (second-hand, one retelling), the letter to the public-works official (single quotation via a critic, tone of mockery, not scored), the Wafd membership, and award claims that differ between sources (honorable mention in 1920 versus gold medal in 1929 per Mathaf, other sites give different awards). COUNTER-VOICES: Ryan's view that the symbolism swamped the sculpture and that his style stayed academic French. SELF-CALIBRATION: three rows, all lowered (persistence 68/0.54 to 64/0.48, impact_motivation 66/0.50 to 62/0.44, resourcefulness 56/0.40 to 52/0.36). SPARSE three-row profile by design; no creative_originality, aesthetic or collaboration row because the open sources do not describe his working method or his dealings with colleagues.
